Lesson 1 · Chapter 14

Male Reproductive Structures

How can sperm delivery fail while testosterone is still present?

Required time
90 minutes
Advanced Learning
24 optional minutes

Learning goal

Trace reproductive structures and distinguish cell production, support, secretion and transport in a fictional case.

Before you begin

Cells form tissues, and tissues form organs. A signal travels from a source to a responsive target; a transport duct and a blood vessel can carry different materials along different routes.

In the textbook

Chapter 14 · 478–481 #1–6; 485 #3,5; 492 #18

Open at p. 478

Four anchor words

Start with four words

These four anchors will help you enter the lesson. The full list below includes the supporting terms.

seminiferous tubules
Coiled tubes inside the testes where sperm cells develop among supporting cells.
Sertoli cells
Supporting cells within the sperm-producing tubes of a testis; they nourish developing sperm and regulate their local conditions.
interstitial cells
Cells between the sperm-producing tubes of a testis that release the hormone testosterone into blood; also called Leydig cells.
vas deferens
A muscular duct that transports sperm from the epididymis toward the ejaculatory duct; also called the ductus deferens.

Learn · Part 1

Compartments of the testes

testes
Paired reproductive organs that support sperm development and release hormones, including testosterone.
seminiferous tubules
Coiled tubes inside the testes where sperm cells develop among supporting cells.
Sertoli cells
Supporting cells within the sperm-producing tubes of a testis; they nourish developing sperm and regulate their local conditions.
interstitial cells
Cells between the sperm-producing tubes of a testis that release the hormone testosterone into blood; also called Leydig cells.
testosterone
A chemical messenger made mainly by cells between the sperm-producing tubes of the testes; it contributes to reproductive development, function and feedback.
model
A simplified representation used to explain observations or make testable predictions under stated assumptions.
observation
Information recorded using a specified method; an explanation of its cause is an inference.

The testes perform two linked jobs: they support sperm development and release hormones. Most sperm development occurs inside seminiferous tubules, the tightly coiled tubes within each testis. Developing germ cells lie among Sertoli cells in the tubule wall. Sertoli cells provide nutrients, organize the local environment and help regulate development. Mature stages move toward the open centre of the tubule before leaving it.

Interstitial cells, also called Leydig cells, occupy spaces between tubules. They release testosterone into nearby blood vessels when they receive a suitable hormonal signal. This arrangement separates the site of hormone production from the site where sperm develop. A sperm cell is a reproductive cell; a Sertoli or interstitial cell supports reproduction through a different role. None of these terms names the entire testis.

The scrotum is the external pouch containing the testes. Its position and temperature-regulating responses help maintain conditions suited to sperm production. Temperature is one influence among several. If a model shows few developing sperm, examine the tubule environment, supporting cells and signals before identifying a cause. Evidence that testosterone is present does not establish that every stage of sperm development is working.

Worked example

A fictional tissue sample has intact interstitial cells but disrupted Sertoli-cell support. Testosterone is detected in blood. Does this prove normal sperm development?

  1. Locate the two compartments: interstitial cells lie between tubules; Sertoli cells support germ cells inside tubules.
  2. Connect the blood result to the hormone-producing compartment.
  3. Seek evidence of germ-cell stages inside tubules before judging sperm development.

No. The result supports hormone release, while the supplied tissue evidence suggests a separate support problem. A count of developing germ-cell stages would help test that explanation.

Stop and check

Which observation would more directly test germ-cell development: testosterone in blood or cells at several stages inside tubules?

Compare your thinking

Cells at several stages inside tubules address development directly. Testosterone provides relevant signalling evidence but does not measure every developmental step.

Advanced LearningWhy one measurement can miss a failure6 minutes

Why one measurement can miss a failure

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced compartments of the testes. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

Biological systems have linked steps, but each step has its own conditions. A hormone assay samples a circulating signal. A tissue image samples structures at one location and time. Neither observation gives a complete view by itself. Pairing the two can narrow a model: preserved hormone release plus altered tubule structure supports a local support hypothesis. Repeated observations and a suitable reference are still needed to distinguish persistent change from sampling error.

Pair the measurements because they sample different links in the pathway. A preserved signal and an altered target compartment can coexist; neither result cancels the other. Repeating both observations against a suitable reference tests whether the apparent mismatch persists.

In the related worked example: No. The result supports hormone release, while the supplied tissue evidence suggests a separate support problem. A count of developing germ-cell stages would help test that explanation. A single assay or image does not establish overall fertility.

Learn · Part 2

The transport pathway

epididymis
A coiled duct where sperm mature and are stored after leaving the testes.
vas deferens
A muscular duct that transports sperm from the epididymis toward the ejaculatory duct; also called the ductus deferens.
ejaculatory duct
A short duct that carries sperm and seminal-vesicle fluid into the urethra.
urethra
A duct carrying urine and, at different times in typical male anatomy, semen to the exterior.
penis
An external organ containing a urethral passage that can deliver semen.
seminal vesicles
Paired glands that add a substantial part of the fluid in semen; they do not produce sperm.
semen
Fluid containing sperm when present plus secretions from reproductive accessory glands.
fertility
The biological capacity or probability of reproduction, influenced by many interacting factors and not established by one classroom measure.
obstruction
A blockage that reduces movement through a passage; it does not necessarily stop production upstream.
reproductive structures
Organs and tissues involved in forming gametes, transporting them or supporting reproductive processes.
route
The path by which a substance enters or moves through a system.

After leaving the seminiferous tubules, sperm pass into the epididymis, a long coiled duct beside the testis. Here they mature and can be stored. During ejaculation, muscular contractions move sperm into the vas deferens. Each vas joins a duct from a seminal vesicle to form an ejaculatory duct, which empties into the urethra. The urethra carries semen through the penis to the exterior.

The pathway connects different functions. Testicular tubules support production, the epididymis supports maturation and storage, and the remaining ducts support transport and delivery. Accessory secretions join along the route. Urine and semen use part of the same urethral passage at different times. The transport diagram therefore needs arrows showing direction, rather than lines that simply connect nearby structures.

Consider a fictional obstruction in a vas deferens. Sperm may still develop upstream while delivery through that duct is reduced. Testosterone can still enter the blood because hormone release follows a separate route. To test the transport explanation, compare evidence from before and after the proposed obstruction. A downstream sample alone cannot distinguish failed production from a blocked passage.

Worked example

Sperm are found in a fictional sample taken from the epididymis but are absent downstream of an obstructed vas deferens. Predict one effect and one function that may persist.

  1. Trace epididymis → vas deferens → ejaculatory duct → urethra.
  2. Put the obstruction between the upstream and downstream samples.
  3. Follow testosterone through blood vessels separately from this duct.

Delivery through the affected duct is reduced, although production upstream and hormone release may persist. A unilateral obstruction does not by itself establish the function of the other side.

Stop and check

Does a blocked vas deferens necessarily stop testosterone from reaching the blood?

Compare your thinking

No. Duct transport and hormone release into blood are distinct routes. The obstruction alone supplies no evidence of failed interstitial-cell signalling.

Advanced LearningPaired organs and cautious conclusions6 minutes

Paired organs and cautious conclusions

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced the transport pathway. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

A diagram often shows one simplified route even when the body has paired structures. If a case describes only one vas deferens, conclusions must remain scoped to that duct. The other route may contribute sperm to an ejaculate. This is why a schematic prediction about one blockage differs from a conclusion about overall fertility. State which structure was observed, which side was tested and which unmeasured route could alter the outcome.

Trace each side separately before combining their outputs. A blockage can leave upstream production intact while changing the contribution that reaches the shared outlet. The location of a sample therefore determines which branch of the transport explanation it can support.

In the related worked example: Delivery through the affected duct is reduced, although production upstream and hormone release may persist. A unilateral obstruction does not by itself establish the function of the other side. A unilateral observation cannot determine the function of both sides.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Paired organs and cautious conclusions — comparison
Case or measureBiological interpretation
Affected ductA local obstruction limits delivery along that route.
Other ductIts contribution remains unmeasured in a one-sided case.

Limitation: A unilateral observation cannot determine the function of both sides.

Learn · Part 3

Semen and accessory glands

prostate gland
A male accessory gland that contributes fluid to semen.
Cowper glands
Small glands below the prostate that release fluid into the urethra; also called bulbourethral glands.
spermatozoon
A specialized sperm cell carrying one chromosome set and able, under suitable conditions, to interact with a developing egg cell.

Semen is a mixture of sperm and secretions from reproductive glands. The paired seminal vesicles lie behind the bladder, which stores urine. They contribute much of its fluid and substances including fructose, which can support sperm energy needs. The prostate surrounds the upper part of the urethra below the bladder and adds fluid containing enzymes and other substances. These secretions change the transport medium; the glands themselves do not produce sperm.

Cowper glands, also called bulbourethral glands, lie near the base of the penis below the prostate. Their mucus helps lubricate the urethral passage and modify its local conditions. The exact composition of an ejaculate reflects contributions from several sites. It is therefore more useful to connect each gland with a contribution than to describe semen as the product of a single organ.

Suppose a model sample contains glandular fluid but no sperm. This observation shows that some secretory and delivery functions occurred. It leaves at least two broad possibilities: sperm production was reduced, or sperm did not reach the sampled passage. Follow the pathway and seek a further observation that distinguishes those explanations. Do not treat the presence of fluid as proof that every reproductive step is intact.

Worked example

A fictional ejaculate contains fluid with fructose but no observed sperm. A student writes, “The seminal vesicles failed to produce sperm.” Repair the explanation.

  1. Separate the fluid contribution from the reproductive cells.
  2. Assign fructose-containing fluid to an accessory-gland contribution and sperm development to testicular tubules.
  3. Keep production and delivery failures as alternatives until another observation distinguishes them.

The seminal vesicles contribute fluid; they do not produce sperm. The sample is consistent with gland secretion plus reduced sperm production or delivery, but it does not identify a single cause.

Stop and check

Why is “semen cell” an inaccurate label?

Compare your thinking

Semen is a mixture containing cells and gland secretions. A spermatozoon is one cell within that mixture.

Advanced LearningMixtures require more than one measure6 minutes

Mixtures require more than one measure

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced semen and accessory glands. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

A sample can change in volume, cell concentration, total cell number or the behaviour of its cells. These are related measurements, not interchangeable labels. For example, concentration is a count per volume, whereas total number also depends on the sampled volume. A classroom model should state what was measured before comparing samples. Avoid turning one measurement into a diagnosis or treating a reference value as a sharp boundary between possible and impossible reproduction.

Equal concentrations do not imply equal total cell numbers if sample volumes differ. Conversely, a dilute larger sample can contain the same total number as a smaller concentrated sample. Neither calculation measures motility or identifies where a production or delivery problem began.

In the related worked example: The seminal vesicles contribute fluid; they do not produce sperm. The sample is consistent with gland secretion plus reduced sperm production or delivery, but it does not identify a single cause. Fluid composition alone cannot diagnose the source of absent sperm.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Mixtures require more than one measure — comparison
Case or measureBiological interpretation
ConcentrationCells counted per unit volume.
Total numberConcentration multiplied by the sampled volume.

Limitation: Fluid composition alone cannot diagnose the source of absent sperm.

Learn · Part 4

Reproductive development and health

Y chromosome
A sex chromosome that typically carries a testis-development signal in humans; its presence alone does not establish every sex trait.
responsive target
A cell or tissue with the receptors and internal machinery needed to respond to a particular signal.
STI
An infection that can be transmitted through sexual contact; pathogens, symptoms, prevention, testing, and treatment differ.
timing
The position and order of events relative to a clearly stated starting point or interval.
embryo
A developing organism in an early stage of organ formation; human stage labels must specify the dating convention.

Early embryos have tissues that can develop along different paths. A gene is a region of DNA whose activity helps produce a biological product or effect. In a typical XY pathway, the SRY gene on the Y chromosome helps start testis development. It works through other genes and cells. SRY does not build every reproductive structure on its own.

Developing testes release testosterone and anti-Müllerian hormone, called AMH. Testosterone supports the growth of certain internal ducts. Some target tissues convert it to DHT, a stronger androgen that helps shape typical external structures. AMH causes another set of embryonic ducts to shrink. Without these testis signals, those ducts can form the uterine tubes and uterus. Ovaries also develop through active gene networks. Their growth is not a process with no gene control.

A signal needs a target that can respond at the right time. A receptor is a cell component that detects a signal and helps start a response. Changes in genes, hormone supply, receptors or timing can alter development. A chromosome image shows only part of this pathway. It cannot establish every body feature, fertility outcome, health need or identity. In a fictional case, separate what was observed from what you inferred.

A sexually transmitted infection, or STI, can affect reproductive function after development. Infection may cause swelling and damage to a passage or its lining. Some infections cause few clear symptoms. Damage can make transport less effective, but infection does not always cause infertility. When judging an information programme, check its evidence and clear wording. Also consider privacy, access, community views, environmental effects, resources and cost. These include social, cultural, ethical and economic concerns.

Worked example

In a fictional developmental model, a hormone is present but one target tissue cannot respond to it. A chromosome image is also available. What additional evidence matters most for the proposed signalling mechanism?

  1. Identify the proposed hormone and target tissue.
  2. Check whether the target has a working response pathway during the relevant developmental interval.
  3. Separate observed chromosomes and hormone levels from inferred anatomical effects.

Evidence about target response and timing is needed. Hormone presence and chromosomes alone do not establish the final structure. Different signals also act on different developmental tissues.

Stop and check

Could the same chromosome pattern support different developmental outcomes when target responses differ?

Compare your thinking

Yes. Gene activity, signal production, target response and timing contribute to development. A chromosome pattern is only part of that evidence.

Advanced LearningDevelopmental pathways are networks6 minutes

Developmental pathways are networks

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced reproductive development and health. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

SRY participates in a regulatory network rather than acting as a one-step switch for every structure. Different tissues respond to different signals at different times. A change in one pathway can therefore affect some structures while leaving others relatively unchanged. Use a network diagram to keep gene activity, hormone production and target response separate. This approach supports a precise biological explanation while avoiding unsupported claims about a person's identity, health needs or future fertility.

Keep measured traits separate. Chromosome patterns, genes, reproductive organs, hormone levels and fertility describe different biological features. Gender identity also has personal and social dimensions that cannot be read from an anatomy image or hormone result. Report the actual observation, such as a chromosome pattern or target-cell response, rather than using it to infer identity, behaviour or worth. A pathway predicts a relationship under stated conditions. It does not make every body identical. A genetic change, different cell lineages within one body, environmental conditions or an intervention can change a particular trait. In a fictional case, name the step supported by evidence and the alternative that remains possible. Identify a further observation that would distinguish them. The classroom model does not establish a diagnosis or an appropriate treatment.

The paired embryonic ducts that respond to testosterone are often called Wolffian ducts. Some target tissues convert testosterone to dihydrotestosterone, or DHT, for particular external-development responses. A hormone effect still depends on a working receptor and suitable timing. The names locate parts of the pathway; they cannot by themselves explain every person’s anatomy. Human papillomavirus, or HPV, names a group of viruses with effects different from the bacteria discussed in core teaching. Persistent infection with certain high-risk HPV types can contribute to cancers. An infection or test result does not establish a person’s character or identify the exact time or source of transmission. Compare the pathogen, tissue, duration and evidence rather than treating all STIs as one process.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Developmental pathways are networks — comparison
Case or measureBiological interpretation
Signal productionA tissue releases a hormone.
Target responseA receptor, timing and local pathway permit an effect.

Limitation: A classroom pathway cannot establish a person's identity, diagnosis or treatment.

Question 2

In a fictional model, germ cells are present and testosterone release continues, but the vas deferens is blocked. Trace the route from sperm production to delivery and identify the first disrupted step.

Up to 320 characters can be saved in this response. Longer writing stays visible for copying and revision.

Attempt the question to open the feedback.

One complete response

Sperm develop in seminiferous tubules, mature in the epididymis, then pass through the vas deferens, ejaculatory duct and urethra. The blocked vas disrupts transport after maturation. Continued hormone release does not prove transport is open.

Do not locate testosterone production inside the duct or infer that every downstream absence means failed sperm production.

Lesson 2 · Chapter 14

Spermatogenesis

What changes when a germ cell makes gametes: sets, copies, shape or signals?

Required time
120 minutes
Advanced Learning
24 optional minutes

Learning goal

Track sperm development through chromosome reduction, differentiation and hormone feedback with explicit cell boundaries.

Before you begin

A chromosome carries DNA. A set contains one of each chromosome type; replication makes sister copies without adding homologous sets. Hormones act through suitable target responses.

In the textbook

Chapter 14 · 495 #19; 502 #2,7,8

Open at p. 495

Four anchor words

Start with four words

These four anchors will help you enter the lesson. The full list below includes the supporting terms.

haploid
Having one chromosome set, conventionally written n.
FSH
Follicle-stimulating hormone: a signal from the anterior pituitary that supports growth of the cells around a developing egg and acts through Sertoli cells to support sperm development.
LH
Luteinizing hormone: a signal from the anterior pituitary that stimulates testosterone release in testes and helps trigger egg release and formation of temporary hormone-producing tissue in ovaries.
negative feedback
Control in which a response reduces the original deviation or lowers upstream stimulation.

Learn · Part 1

Gametes and chromosome sets

diploid
Having two chromosome sets, conventionally written 2n.
haploid
Having one chromosome set, conventionally written n.
spermatogonium
A precursor cell in the sperm-producing lineage with two chromosome sets; its divisions can maintain precursor cells and produce cells that develop toward sperm.
primary spermatocyte
A diploid germ cell that has replicated its DNA and enters meiosis I during spermatogenesis.
fertilization
A sequence in which sperm and oocyte membranes and genetic material combine to begin development of a zygote.
zygote
The diploid cell formed after fertilization and combination of parental chromosome sets.

A chromosome carries a long DNA molecule with associated proteins. A set contains one representative of each chromosome type. Typical human body cells are diploid: they contain two sets, with 46 chromosomes in total. Gametes are haploid, carrying one set of 23. Fertilization combines two haploid contributions, restoring two sets in the zygote. This avoids doubling the number of sets in each generation.

A spermatogonium is an early germ cell that can divide by mitosis, the process that usually preserves chromosome sets in daughter cells. A cell entering sperm-producing meiosis becomes a primary spermatocyte. Before the meiotic divisions, it replicates its DNA. Each chromosome then consists of two joined sister chromatids. The cell still has 46 chromosomes and two sets, although its DNA amount has doubled.

Track sets and copies separately. Meiosis I separates corresponding homologous chromosomes, reducing each product to one set. Meiosis II separates the sister chromatids. A diagram should state whether its counts refer to the original cell, one daughter cell or all products combined. Calling a replicated primary spermatocyte tetraploid would confuse extra DNA copies with extra homologous sets.

Worked example

A primary spermatocyte has completed DNA replication. Count human chromosome sets, chromosomes and DNA molecules before meiosis I and in one product after meiosis I.

  1. Begin with two homologous sets and 46 chromosomes.
  2. Replication creates two chromatids per chromosome: 92 DNA molecules, still two sets.
  3. Meiosis I separates homologues: each product has one set, 23 chromosomes and 46 DNA molecules.

Before meiosis I: 2 sets, 46 chromosomes, 92 DNA molecules. After meiosis I, per cell: 1 set, 23 chromosomes, 46 DNA molecules.

Stop and check

Why does DNA replication not make this cell tetraploid?

Compare your thinking

It adds sister copies of existing chromosomes, not extra homologous sets. Ploidy counts sets, so the cell remains diploid.

Advanced LearningCounting depends on the boundary6 minutes

Counting depends on the boundary

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced gametes and chromosome sets. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

During division, counts can differ depending on whether the boundary encloses the whole cell, one pole or one daughter nucleus. Label the boundary before doing arithmetic. The chromosome count also changes when sister centromeres separate, even before the cell divides. This does not mean the species has acquired a new stable ploidy. A stage table should name both the biological event and the region being counted.

DNA copying and orderly separation help transmit genetic information. Variation can come from new combinations as well as new DNA changes. During meiosis, paired chromosomes can exchange corresponding DNA segments, and different pairs can separate in different combinations. Which sperm and egg combine adds another source of variation. These processes reshuffle existing gene versions. A mutation changes DNA itself. Family resemblance therefore does not mean genetic identity, and a probability does not guarantee a particular offspring.

Keep a separate ledger for sets, centromeres and DNA molecules. Homolog separation reduces the number of sets per daughter cell, while sister copies remain joined. An apparent doubling during anaphase must be tied to the whole-cell boundary before comparing it with a daughter nucleus. Counts are per stated cell and stage, not a change in species ploidy.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Learn · Part 2

Division and differentiation

secondary spermatocyte
A haploid cell produced by meiosis I that proceeds through meiosis II during spermatogenesis.
spermatid
A haploid cell produced by meiosis II that differentiates into a sperm cell.
acrosome
A specialized cap on the sperm head involved in interaction with the oocyte's coverings.
flagellum
A long cellular extension that produces movement, as in the tail of a sperm cell.
oocyte
A developing female germ cell; stage names such as primary and secondary oocyte reflect meiotic state.
differentiation
The regulated process through which cells develop specialized gene-expression patterns, structures, and functions.

One primary spermatocyte normally completes two meiotic divisions. Meiosis I produces two secondary spermatocytes, each with 23 duplicated chromosomes in the human model. Meiosis II separates the sister chromatids, producing four haploid spermatids. Each spermatid has 23 unduplicated chromosomes. The sequence reduces chromosome sets once, then separates the remaining copies without another round of DNA replication.

Spermatids must also change their structure. During differentiation, their nuclei become more compact, a flagellum develops, and excess cytoplasm is removed. The flagellum is the tail-like structure involved in movement. Mitochondria near its base support energy transfer. The acrosome is a specialized structure over part of the head that supports interaction with the oocyte's coverings. These changes produce spermatozoa, or differentiated sperm cells.

Differentiation changes cell form and function; it does not halve chromosome number again. Later maturation in the epididymis and changes within the reproductive tract support further functional readiness. A sperm may have the usual chromosome number yet show reduced movement or an impaired acrosome. Describe the affected step before predicting a downstream consequence. Shape, chromosome count and successful fertilization require different kinds of evidence.

Watch and make sense of it

Worked example

One typical primary spermatocyte completes both meiotic divisions. Predict the immediate products and explain why they still need further change.

  1. Meiosis I produces two secondary spermatocytes with duplicated chromosomes.
  2. Meiosis II separates sister chromatids, producing four haploid spermatids.
  3. Differentiation reshapes each spermatid, including its acrosome, compact nucleus and flagellum.

The immediate products are four haploid spermatids. Meiosis establishes their chromosome content; differentiation and later maturation support the form and functions associated with sperm.

Stop and check

Does forming a flagellum require another reduction division?

Compare your thinking

No. Flagellum formation is part of cell differentiation. The reduction in chromosome sets has already occurred during meiosis I.

Advanced LearningOne lineage is a model, not a yield guarantee6 minutes

One lineage is a model, not a yield guarantee

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced division and differentiation. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

A four-product diagram follows one successful meiotic lineage. It does not predict that every early germ cell becomes four functional sperm or that all later steps succeed. Cells may be lost during development, and maturation adds further requirements. Keep the lineage count distinct from a measured production rate. A production-rate study would also need elapsed time, a defined sampled region and a method for distinguishing developmental stages.

A lineage diagram answers how division distributes chromosomes, not how many mature sperm a tissue releases each day. To estimate a rate, count suitable stages over a defined interval and distinguish surviving products from earlier cells that did not complete development.

In the related worked example: The immediate products are four haploid spermatids. Meiosis establishes their chromosome content; differentiation and later maturation support the form and functions associated with sperm. Four immediate products do not guarantee four functional sperm.

Learn · Part 3

Hormone sources and targets

GnRH
Gonadotropin-releasing hormone: a chemical signal from the brain region called the hypothalamus that stimulates release of FSH and LH from the front part of the pituitary gland.
FSH
Follicle-stimulating hormone: a signal from the anterior pituitary that supports growth of the cells around a developing egg and acts through Sertoli cells to support sperm development.
LH
Luteinizing hormone: a signal from the anterior pituitary that stimulates testosterone release in testes and helps trigger egg release and formation of temporary hormone-producing tissue in ovaries.
hypothalamus
A brain region that integrates information and releases signals to help regulate the pituitary gland.
anterior pituitary
The hormone-producing front part of the pituitary gland below the brain.
primary sex characteristic
A structure directly involved in reproduction, such as an ovary or testis.
secondary sex characteristic
A pubertal trait influenced by hormones that is not itself a gamete-producing or gamete-transporting organ.
muscle
Tissue specialized for contraction and force production.

Hormones coordinate sperm production with activity elsewhere in the body. The hypothalamus, a region of the brain, releases gonadotropin-releasing hormone, or GnRH. This signal stimulates the anterior pituitary gland to release FSH and LH. FSH means follicle-stimulating hormone, and LH means luteinizing hormone. Their names reflect ovarian functions, but both also act in the testicular pathway.

FSH supports Sertoli-cell functions within the seminiferous tubules. LH stimulates interstitial cells to produce testosterone. Testosterone acts with other signals to support reproductive tissues and sperm development. It also influences several secondary sex characteristics during puberty, including changes in muscle, hair growth and voice. Primary sex characteristics are structures directly involved in reproduction. Secondary characteristics develop particularly during puberty and are not themselves gamete-producing or transport organs.

Keep source, signal, target and response in order. For example, write anterior pituitary → LH → interstitial cell → testosterone release. Testosterone then reaches responsive tissues through the blood. Its concentration alone does not reveal every target response. A cell without an effective receptor may respond weakly even when the signal is present. This distinction helps explain why one hormone measurement cannot diagnose an entire pathway.

GnRH reaches the anterior pituitary through connecting blood vessels. FSH and LH then travel in blood to their target tissues. They stimulate responses; they do not turn into testosterone or other reproductive hormones. A complete pathway therefore names the source, the signal carried in blood and the responding cell. It keeps hormone movement separate from sperm movement through a duct.

Worked example

In a simplified pathway, GnRH stimulates the anterior pituitary, which releases LH. Identify the next target and response, then contrast the FSH branch.

  1. Trace GnRH from hypothalamus to anterior pituitary.
  2. Trace LH to interstitial cells and testosterone release.
  3. Trace FSH to Sertoli-cell support within seminiferous tubules; connect this branch with local testosterone action.

LH acts on interstitial cells to support testosterone production. FSH acts through Sertoli cells to support germ-cell development. The branches interact but do not have identical targets.

Stop and check

Which label is wrong in “FSH from the testes acts on the anterior pituitary”?

Compare your thinking

Both the stated source and direction are wrong for this pathway. FSH is released by the anterior pituitary and acts on Sertoli cells in the testes.

Advanced LearningSignals can interact at a target6 minutes

Signals can interact at a target

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced hormone sources and targets. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

An arrow diagram can make each hormone look sufficient by itself. In reality, a target's response can depend on several signals and its local environment. FSH-related support and local testosterone action help illustrate that interaction. To test one contribution in a model, vary that signal while keeping the other conditions comparable. A weaker response after one change supports a contribution; it does not show that the altered signal is the only cause of the response.

A controlled comparison changes one branch while keeping the other as comparable as possible. A reduced response then supports a contribution from the changed signal. Because the branches interact locally, it does not demonstrate that either hormone alone is sufficient for every developmental step.

In the related worked example: LH acts on interstitial cells to support testosterone production. FSH acts through Sertoli cells to support germ-cell development. The branches interact but do not have identical targets. A one-arrow model omits interacting signals and local conditions.

Learn · Part 4

Feedback and evidence

negative feedback
Control in which a response reduces the original deviation or lowers upstream stimulation.
inhibin
A gonadal hormone that provides feedback reducing FSH release.
controlled variable
A factor intentionally kept consistent so it does not confound the tested comparison.
feedback suppression
Reduction of an upstream signal when a downstream response feeds back on its source.
variables
Features that can change, be controlled or be measured in an investigation.
comparison
Examination of similarities and differences between specified conditions or observations.
data
Recorded observations or measurements with their context, units and method.
anabolic steroid
A steroid substance with actions related to testosterone; an outside androgen signal can alter feedback and suppress normal sperm production.
growth hormone
A protein hormone released by the anterior pituitary that contributes to growth and metabolism; also called hGH or somatotropin.
andropause
A term sometimes used for age-associated testicular hormone changes; it does not mean an abrupt universal cessation of sperm production.

Negative feedback occurs when a response reduces the change that initiated it. In the testicular pathway, testosterone can reduce upstream hypothalamic and pituitary signalling. Sertoli cells also release inhibin, a signal that reduces pituitary FSH release. These feedback routes connect downstream activity with earlier control points. The word negative describes the direction of regulation, rather than judging the response as harmful.

Consider a synthetic comparison in which testosterone decreases while LH increases. Reduced testosterone feedback could permit more LH release. The pattern is consistent with reduced testicular production or response, rather than a simple absence of pituitary stimulation. It does not uniquely establish a cause: timing, receptor function and other evidence could alter the explanation. Compare repeated measurements collected under stated conditions.

A controlled variable is a condition kept similar while another factor is compared. In a model study, hold the measurement method and sampling interval constant. Predict what would happen to the upstream signal if feedback became weaker, then compare that prediction with the data. A useful explanation names the observed change, the feedback mechanism and one observation that would challenge it.

An anabolic steroid is a steroid substance with actions related to testosterone. An outside androgen signal can suppress upstream signals through negative feedback and reduce normal sperm production. This shows why more circulating androgen action need not mean more sperm. Human growth hormone, or hGH, is a protein hormone made by the pituitary. It is not a steroid, despite being grouped with steroids on one supplied slide.

Testosterone patterns can also change with age, health and other conditions. The term andropause is sometimes used for age-related changes, but it should not imply one abrupt, universal end to sperm production. A symptom such as tiredness has many possible explanations. In a scientific case, compare repeated measurements and the stated context rather than inferring a specific hormone condition from age or one symptom alone.

Worked example

In a simplified intact feedback model, testosterone action falls while hypothalamic and pituitary responses remain functional. Predict the direction of LH change and state a condition on that prediction.

  1. Identify testosterone's negative-feedback influence on upstream signalling.
  2. Reduce that inhibitory influence in the model.
  3. Predict increased upstream drive and LH, provided the relevant tissues can respond.

LH is expected to rise in this bounded model. The prediction may fail if the pituitary cannot respond or if another signal changes the pathway.

Stop and check

Does negative feedback mean every hormone in the loop always decreases?

Compare your thinking

No. It describes how the response opposes a change. Reducing an inhibitory signal can increase an upstream hormone.

Advanced LearningFeedback observations need timing6 minutes

Feedback observations need timing

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced feedback and evidence. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

A feedback prediction concerns a response over time. A single simultaneous blood sample may capture a delay, pulse or transition instead of a settled state. Compare repeated measurements with a timeline and a reference condition. Inhibin also provides a more targeted feedback influence on FSH, so LH and FSH need not move together in every case. Treat a simple loop as a testable explanation with stated assumptions, not a universal diagnostic rule.

Place the proposed fall in testosterone action before the predicted pituitary response on the timeline. Samples taken during a delay may not yet show the settled feedback direction. Comparing repeat measurements helps distinguish a transition from a persistent failure of the assumed response.

In the related worked example: LH is expected to rise in this bounded model. The prediction may fail if the pituitary cannot respond or if another signal changes the pathway. The predicted LH rise assumes responsive upstream tissues.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Lesson 3 · Chapter 14

Female Reproductive Structures

Why are fertilization, transport and implantation different steps?

Required time
105 minutes
Advanced Learning

Learning goal

Trace oocyte development and movement while distinguishing the oocyte, follicle, corpus luteum and uterine lining.

Before you begin

A reproductive cell is distinct from its supporting tissue. Meiosis reduces chromosome sets, while cytoplasmic division can be unequal. A structure's location helps explain its function.

Learn · Part 1

Ovaries and supporting tissues

ovary
A reproductive organ that contains developing egg cells and releases reproductive hormones.
follicle
An ovarian structure containing an oocyte and surrounding support and hormone-producing cells.
corpus luteum
Temporary hormone-producing tissue formed from a follicle after ovulation; it releases progesterone and estrogen.
secondary oocyte
The cell produced after meiosis I in oogenesis; in humans it is typically arrested in metaphase II until fertilization.
ovulation
Release of a secondary oocyte and surrounding cells from a mature ovarian follicle.
estrogen
A class of steroid hormones involved in reproductive-tissue function, secondary sex characteristics, cycle regulation, and feedback.
progesterone
A steroid hormone that supports secretory endometrial conditions, pregnancy-related changes, and reproductive feedback.

An ovary contains developing oocytes and the tissues that support them. An oocyte is a developing female germ cell. A follicle contains that cell together with surrounding support cells. As a follicle develops, its cells and the oocyte change in coordinated ways. The follicle can contribute hormones to the blood, while the oocyte carries the chromosome contribution for possible fertilization.

Ovulation releases a secondary oocyte from a mature follicle. The remaining follicular tissue stays in the ovary and develops into the corpus luteum. This temporary endocrine structure releases progesterone and estrogen after ovulation. If it does not receive pregnancy-related support, it usually regresses. The released oocyte and the corpus luteum therefore have different locations, structures and roles.

Use the tissue boundary when labelling an image. A label pointing to the oocyte should identify the cell, while a follicle label includes its supporting tissue. A corpus-luteum label refers to tissue remaining after release. Confusing these labels makes later hormone explanations difficult. For example, progesterone production after ovulation does not require the released oocyte to remain inside the corpus luteum.

Worked example

An ovarian diagram shows a large follicle containing an oocyte and, elsewhere, a corpus luteum. A student labels both structures “eggs.” Correct the diagram.

  1. Locate the oocyte inside its surrounding follicular cells.
  2. Label the follicle as a supporting structure containing the oocyte.
  3. Label the corpus luteum as tissue formed from the follicle after ovulation, with a hormone-secreting role.

The oocyte is the reproductive cell. A follicle includes that cell and supporting tissues; a corpus luteum is the later secretory structure, not a second egg.

Stop and check

What changes into the corpus luteum after ovulation: the released oocyte or the remaining follicular tissue?

Compare your thinking

The remaining follicular tissue changes into the corpus luteum. The released oocyte travels separately.

Advanced LearningImages compress different times6 minutes

Images compress different times

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced ovaries and supporting tissues. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

An ovary diagram may place several follicular stages side by side to teach a sequence. It is not necessarily a literal photograph of one person's ovary at one moment. Read the figure's purpose and use stage arrows to separate a time sequence from physical position. A structure's size or colour may also be exaggerated for visibility. The biologically important relationships are the oocyte within its support tissue and the follicle's change after ovulation.

Use arrows to translate the side-by-side image into a time sequence. That prevents a change in one follicle from being mistaken for two identical reproductive cells present at once. Labels for cell, surrounding tissue and later structure should remain distinct even in a simplified diagram.

In the related worked example: The oocyte is the reproductive cell. A follicle includes that cell and supporting tissues; a corpus luteum is the later secretory structure, not a second egg. A composite teaching image need not represent one ovary at one instant.

Learn · Part 2

Transport and implantation surfaces

Fallopian tube
A uterine tube that receives an ovulated oocyte and is the usual site of fertilization; its lining and muscular wall support transport toward the uterus.
fimbriae
Finger-like extensions near the opening of a uterine tube that help receive an ovulated oocyte.
uterus
A muscular reproductive organ containing the endometrium and supporting implantation and prenatal development.
endometrium
The hormone-responsive inner lining of the uterus where implantation may occur.
cervix
The lower, narrow region of the uterus that opens into the vagina.
vagina
A muscular canal connecting the cervix with the exterior.
blastocyst
An early developmental stage with an outer trophoblast, inner cell mass, and fluid-filled cavity.
implantation
Attachment and embedding of a hatched blastocyst in a receptive uterine endometrium.

The Fallopian tubes, also called uterine tubes, extend from near the ovaries toward the uterus. Finger-like fimbriae near each ovarian end help direct the released oocyte toward the tube. Cilia are tiny moving projections on cells lining the passage. Together with muscular activity, they support transport. The ovary is close to the tube's opening but is not joined to it by a sealed internal duct.

Fertilization usually occurs within a uterine tube. An early developing conceptus then moves toward the uterus, a muscular organ with an inner lining called the endometrium. The endometrium changes across the reproductive cycle and can support implantation when receptive. The cervix forms the lower uterine opening into the vagina. The vagina receives semen during intercourse and forms part of the birth passage.

Trace the order of movement on a labelled diagram. Oocyte release, sperm transport, fertilization and implantation are distinct events. Evidence that ovulation occurred does not prove that the tube was open or that implantation followed. To investigate an obstruction, identify which events occur upstream and which require passage through the affected region. Keep the usual location of fertilization separate from the later implantation surface.

Worked example

A fictional zygote is in a uterine tube. Trace its usual route toward the implantation surface and explain why the cervix is not that surface.

  1. Follow the uterine tube toward the uterine cavity.
  2. Identify the endometrium as the uterine lining associated with implantation.
  3. Place the cervix at the lower uterine opening into the vagina, not along the normal tube-to-endometrium implantation sequence.

Early development and transport proceed toward the uterus, where the blastocyst can implant in the endometrium. Fertilization and implantation are different events at different usual locations.

Stop and check

Is the ovary normally joined to the uterine tube by a closed duct carrying the oocyte all the way?

Compare your thinking

No. Fimbriae and local movement help bring the released oocyte into the tube. A simplified diagram should not imply an uninterrupted closed ovarian duct.

Advanced LearningTransport is active and coordinated6 minutes

Transport is active and coordinated

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced transport and implantation surfaces. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

A transport arrow summarizes several mechanisms. Ciliary activity and muscular movement contribute to movement within the uterine tube, while developmental events continue during transit. A structural change may alter timing as well as whether passage occurs. This is why an explanation of transport should include the tissue function and the stage being moved. A classroom case can test that relationship without assuming that every delayed transit produces the same clinical outcome.

Track both position and developmental stage along the route. Movement is not just a change of address: it must be coordinated with continuing development. A proposed transport disruption therefore needs evidence about tissue function and timing, not merely an arrow drawn between two locations.

In the related worked example: Early development and transport proceed toward the uterus, where the blastocyst can implant in the endometrium. Fertilization and implantation are different events at different usual locations. A delayed transit does not by itself establish one clinical outcome.

Learn · Part 3

Oogenesis and meiotic pauses

primary oocyte
A developing oocyte that has entered meiosis I and may remain arrested in prophase I for years.
polar body
A small haploid cell produced by unequal cytokinesis during oogenesis that usually does not become an egg.
meiotic completion
Finishing a meiotic division; in a typical human secondary oocyte, meiosis II completes after sperm-triggered activation.

Oogenesis is the development of oocytes. In humans, primary oocytes begin meiosis before birth, then pause in the first division. From puberty onward, some follicles develop during each reproductive cycle. An oocyte usually finishes meiosis I shortly before ovulation. The chromosomes separate, but the cytoplasm does not split equally. One large secondary oocyte forms, along with a small polar body.

The secondary oocyte begins meiosis II, then usually pauses at metaphase II. This is its stage when released at ovulation. It has one set of chromosomes, but each chromosome still has two joined sister chromatids. Sperm entry normally triggers the rest of meiosis II. The cytoplasm again splits unequally. The maternal and paternal chromosome sets can then come together. Polar bodies receive chromosomes but little cytoplasm. They usually do not become functional gametes.

Compare this sequence with spermatogenesis. Both use meiosis to reduce the number of chromosome sets. Spermatogenesis usually forms four similar-sized spermatids, which then change shape and mature. Oogenesis keeps most resources in one large cell and includes long pauses. Equal sharing of chromosomes does not require equal cell sizes. Count at a named stage: the secondary oocyte released at ovulation has 23 duplicated chromosomes. It has not yet finished meiosis II.

Worked example

Compare a typical human primary oocyte before completion of meiosis I with the secondary oocyte released at ovulation. State the pause and chromosome-copy condition.

  1. The primary oocyte has replicated chromosomes and is paused in prophase I.
  2. Completion of meiosis I separates homologues through an unequal cytoplasmic division.
  3. The secondary oocyte is haploid with duplicated chromosomes and is typically paused in metaphase II at ovulation.

The primary oocyte has 46 duplicated chromosomes; the secondary oocyte has 23 duplicated chromosomes. Completion of meiosis II normally follows fertilization-related activation, rather than preceding ovulation.

Stop and check

Why does one large secondary oocyte not mean that meiosis I failed to divide the chromosomes equally?

Compare your thinking

Homologues can separate while cytoplasm is divided unequally. Chromosome allocation and cytoplasmic volume are separate features; a polar body receives a chromosome set with little cytoplasm.

Advanced LearningNumber and investment describe different features6 minutes

Number and investment describe different features

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced oogenesis and meiotic pauses. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

Comparing four spermatids with one large female gamete highlights a difference in cytoplasmic allocation. It does not mean that the female meiotic sequence has only one division. Both homolog separation and sister separation remain necessary. The large cell retains resources and cellular machinery for early development. Keep this functional comparison distinct from claims about the total lifetime number, quality or reproductive potential of gametes in an individual.

Compare nuclear events separately from the sharing of cytoplasm. The small polar bodies do not mean a meiotic division was skipped. Retention of cellular machinery helps explain the large gamete's early developmental contribution, without ranking individual gametes by reproductive potential.

In the related worked example: The primary oocyte has 46 duplicated chromosomes; the secondary oocyte has 23 duplicated chromosomes. Completion of meiosis II normally follows fertilization-related activation, rather than preceding ovulation. Immediate product counts are not lifetime output or quality measurements.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Learn · Part 4

Structure and reproductive function

ciliary transport
Movement of material along a surface by coordinated beating of tiny cell extensions called cilia.
fertility probability
The chance of a specified reproductive outcome under stated conditions; it depends on many factors and is not established by one classroom measurement.
revision
A reasoned change to a prediction, explanation or plan after considering evidence or feedback.

Reproduction needs working tissues, hormone support and an open route for transport. Cilia need a healthy lining to move an oocyte. Muscle activity also helps move it along the passage. A blockage may make it harder for gametes to meet or for an early conceptus to reach the uterus. Fertility describes a chance under stated conditions. It does not promise an outcome for one person.

Some infections cause inflammation, followed by scarring. Chlamydia and gonorrhoea can contribute to pelvic inflammatory disease. This condition affects upper reproductive tissues. Scars may change a uterine tube's lining or block its passage. Follow the proposed chain: infection, then tissue damage, then an effect on transport. Each link needs evidence. Not every infection causes damage, and one person's reproductive outcome may have several causes.

Use the fictional cases to investigate production and transport without sharing personal information. Start with this question: can sperm production continue if a duct is blocked? Predict what you would see in the testis and in the passage. Next, record each case's tissue, signal and passage observations. Compare Case T with a case that has an open passage.

Case T has a blocked passage, yet retains observations of germ cells and their support. This means low delivery need not mean low production. Name another observation that could help tell these explanations apart. Then revise your explanation using the evidence. This online task shows your reasoning. It does not certify physical laboratory skills or live teamwork.

Worked example

In the supplied structure dataset, T has germ cells, support cells and LH present but a blocked duct. P has absent germ cells, disrupted support and an open duct. Compare two explanations for reduced sperm delivery.

  1. Record each supplied observation without replacing absent with unmeasured.
  2. For T, connect the blockage with delivery despite evidence of upstream structures.
  3. For P, connect disrupted development/support with reduced production despite an open route.

The dataset supports different proposed mechanisms in T and P. It does not prove normal maturation in T or identify the original cause of the support disruption in P.

Stop and check

A peer says, “Every low downstream sperm count proves a blocked duct.” Which comparison challenges that claim?

Compare your thinking

P has an open duct but lacks observed germ cells and has disrupted support. It supplies an alternative production-related explanation for reduced downstream sperm.

Advanced LearningCommunicating a revised model6 minutes

Communicating a revised model

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced structure and reproductive function. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

A useful revision changes the causal claim, not merely its confidence word. Replace “low delivery means blockage” with “low delivery can result from production, maturation or transport changes.” Then identify which observations favour each branch. A next investigation should discriminate between the remaining branches, such as examining developmental stages upstream. This is independent evaluation of a supplied peer explanation; it does not claim that a learner has demonstrated real-time teamwork or performed a physical laboratory procedure.

The same low-delivery observation fits more than one mechanism. Compare the upstream evidence before selecting a transport-only explanation. A useful additional observation tests whether maturation proceeds in T or which support conditions differ in P, rather than merely repeating the outlet count.

In the related worked example: The dataset supports different proposed mechanisms in T and P. It does not prove normal maturation in T or identify the original cause of the support disruption in P. These cases do not establish normal maturation or the original cause.

Lesson 4 · Chapter 14

Menstrual Cycle

How do changing hormone signals coordinate two different cycles?

Required time
150 minutes
Advanced Learning
30 optional minutes

Learning goal

Align ovarian and uterine events and explain changing feedback using a labelled, qualified graph.

Before you begin

Hormone sources and targets form pathways. Negative feedback opposes a change; positive feedback can reinforce it within defined conditions. Graph axes identify time and the measured quantity.

Learn · Part 1

Two coordinated cycles

ovarian cycle
The sequence of follicular development, ovulation, and luteal activity in the ovaries.
uterine cycle
The recurring changes in the endometrium, including shedding, rebuilding and secretory preparation.
follicular phase
The ovarian-cycle phase during which follicles develop before ovulation.
luteal phase
The ovarian-cycle phase after ovulation when the corpus luteum produces progesterone and estrogen.
menstruation
Shedding of much of the functional endometrial layer after ovarian-hormone support declines in a non-pregnant cycle.
axis
A labelled reference line on a graph indicating a variable and its measurement scale.

The ovarian cycle describes changes in follicles, ovulation and the corpus luteum. The uterine cycle describes changes in the endometrium. During the follicular phase, ovarian follicles develop while estrogen supports rebuilding of the uterine lining. After ovulation, the luteal phase begins as the remaining follicular tissue forms the corpus luteum. These ovarian events coordinate with a more secretory uterine lining.

Menstruation is the shedding of much of the functional endometrial lining. It commonly follows a decline in ovarian steroid support when pregnancy has not sustained the corpus luteum. Menstrual bleeding is usually counted as the start of a new cycle. Follicle recruitment can already be occurring around this transition, so biological events overlap rather than fitting into completely isolated boxes.

An illustrative 28-day cycle helps align events on a shared time axis, but real cycle lengths and ovulation timing vary. A diagram should name both the ovarian event and the uterine response. Saying that the ovary menstruates would place an event in the wrong organ. Saying that ovulation always occurs on one numbered day would treat an example schedule as a universal rule.

Worked example

Place follicle development, ovulation, corpus-luteum function, endometrial rebuilding and secretory maintenance on two aligned tracks in a typical simplified cycle.

  1. Use an ovarian track for follicular phase → ovulation → luteal phase.
  2. Use a uterine track for shedding → rebuilding → secretory maintenance.
  3. Align the tracks by changing hormone signals, rather than calling a uterine event an ovarian structure.

Follicular estrogen supports rebuilding; luteal progesterone supports a secretory endometrium. These coordinated tracks have different events and should remain separately labelled.

Stop and check

Is menstruation the release of an oocyte from its follicle?

Compare your thinking

No. Menstruation is shedding of the uterine lining. Ovulation is release of the oocyte from the ovarian follicle.

Advanced LearningA cycle diagram is a coordinate system6 minutes

A cycle diagram is a coordinate system

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced two coordinated cycles. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

Many diagrams use a 28-day horizontal axis because it is easy to read. The axis is a teaching convention, not a schedule guaranteed for every cycle. Ovarian and uterine events are better aligned by evidence of transitions than by assuming that the same date always marks them. An extended cycle might involve a longer interval before ovulation. That possibility is different from claiming that all stages have stretched by exactly the same proportion.

Align the tracks by biological transitions instead of stretching every interval to fit a fixed calendar. A longer interval before ovulation need not lengthen later phases by the same factor. The two tracks remain causally connected while describing different tissues and events.

In the related worked example: Follicular estrogen supports rebuilding; luteal progesterone supports a secretory endometrium. These coordinated tracks have different events and should remain separately labelled. A 28-day axis is a teaching convention, not an individual schedule.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.

Models and Data Lab: Compare hormone events in time

Learn · Part 2

Follicle growth and changing feedback

positive feedback
Control in which a response amplifies the initiating change until an endpoint interrupts the loop.
LH surge
A brief marked increase in luteinizing hormone associated with final follicular changes and ovulation.
relative concentration
A concentration expressed against a reference scale rather than necessarily in absolute chemical units.
peak
The highest observed value in a defined region or interval; sparse observations may miss the actual maximum.
limitation
A boundary on what a method, dataset or model can establish.

At the start of a cycle, FSH from the pituitary supports follicle growth. Growing follicles release estrogen, which helps rebuild the uterine lining. Estrogen also acts on the brain and pituitary. At many stages, ovarian hormones reduce the release of FSH and LH. These two pituitary hormones are called gonadotropins. Changes in hormone supply and target sensitivity help coordinate follicle growth with the rest of the cycle.

Near ovulation, estrogen stays high long enough to change the feedback response. Under the conditions present at this stage, it increases activity in the hypothalamus and pituitary. A large rise in LH follows. This LH surge helps trigger ovulation and the formation of luteal tissue. Read this sequence in order: a sustained estrogen rise, then an LH surge, then the ovarian response.

Positive feedback strengthens the change that started the response. Here, rising estrogen helps increase an upstream signal instead of reducing it. Estrogen does not always have the same feedback effect. Its level, how long it stays high and the state of its targets all matter. On a pathway diagram, label each arrow as stimulation or inhibition. State the stage of the cycle so the arrow has a clear meaning.

Ovarian hormones also help bring about changes at puberty. Estrogen supports reproductive tissue growth and secondary changes such as breast development. Progesterone works with other signals to support tissues such as the uterine lining. An ovary or uterus is a primary reproductive structure; breast development is a secondary pubertal change. GnRH, FSH and LH act before the ovarian response, as they do in the testis pathway. Timing and growth vary. One visible trait cannot reveal the whole hormone pathway.

Worked example

In the supplied series, estrogen's relative index rises to 10 on day 12 and LH peaks at 18 on day 14. Explain a plausible connection and one limitation of these data.

  1. Find day 12 on the time axis. Read the estrogen index as 10 on its own relative scale.
  2. Find day 14 and read the LH peak as 18 on the LH scale. The LH peak comes after the estrogen rise. Do not compare 18 with 10 as if they were amounts on a shared concentration scale.
  3. Connect the order to the mechanism: sustained high estrogen near ovulation can increase upstream activity through positive feedback, helping produce an LH surge.
  4. State the limit: the sample points are two days apart, and other conditions were not measured. The pattern supports the connection but does not prove an exact trigger level or hour of ovulation.

The pattern is consistent with an estrogen-associated feedback transition preceding an LH surge. The sampled indices do not by themselves prove a universal threshold or the exact hour of ovulation.

Stop and check

Does estrogen always inhibit LH release under every cycle condition?

Compare your thinking

No. Its feedback effect depends on concentration, duration and physiological context. Sustained high estrogen can support the mid-cycle positive-feedback response.

Advanced LearningDuration can matter as well as height6 minutes

Duration can matter as well as height

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced follicle growth and changing feedback. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

A hormone curve has more information than its largest value. Two curves can share a peak but differ in how long they remain elevated. A target response may depend on that exposure history and on earlier signals. When comparing models, plot time clearly and avoid reducing every response to one threshold. A carefully bounded explanation can use both the sustained rise and the later surge while acknowledging that the classroom dataset samples only a few days.

Two signals with equal peaks can have different histories. A target exposed briefly and one exposed for a sustained interval need not respond alike. Interpret the estrogen rise and later LH surge using their order and duration, while distinguishing the few measured points from the unsampled intervals.

In the related worked example: The pattern is consistent with an estrogen-associated feedback transition preceding an LH surge. The sampled indices do not by themselves prove a universal threshold or the exact hour of ovulation. Relative indices do not establish a universal threshold or exact ovulation time.

Learn · Part 3

Corpus luteum and the endometrium

hCG
Human chorionic gonadotropin; a trophoblast-derived hormone that helps maintain corpus-luteum function early in pregnancy.

After ovulation, the corpus luteum releases progesterone and estrogen. Progesterone helps the endometrium maintain secretions and conditions that can support an implanting blastocyst. Trace the link from source to target: corpus luteum, then progesterone, then uterine lining. Ovarian hormones also reduce activity in the hypothalamus and pituitary through negative feedback. One tissue change in the ovary can therefore affect both the uterus and later hormone release.

Without support from an early pregnancy, the corpus luteum usually shrinks. Progesterone and estrogen levels fall. Much of the functional uterine lining then breaks down and is shed as menstrual bleeding. The lower hormone levels also reduce negative feedback on the brain and pituitary. FSH and LH release can change, helping support follicle activity in the next cycle.

Separate two questions. What helps maintain the lining after ovulation? Progesterone does. What helps maintain the corpus luteum in early pregnancy? A signal called hCG does; a later lesson explains its source and role. Keep the tissue, its hormone and its target separate. On a typical cycle graph, link falling ovarian hormones to loss of support for the lining. The graph shows an example pattern, not an exact schedule for everyone.

Worked example

In a cycle without an ongoing pregnancy signal, corpus-luteum function declines. Predict the effect on progesterone support and the endometrium.

  1. Identify the corpus luteum as an important post-ovulation progesterone source.
  2. Follow reduced luteal function to declining hormone support.
  3. Connect withdrawal of support with endometrial breakdown and shedding in the model.

Progesterone support declines, and the maintained endometrium breaks down. The oocyte itself is not the source of the shed uterine tissue.

Stop and check

Would continued strong luteal support fit the same simple explanation for hormone-withdrawal bleeding?

Compare your thinking

No. That observation would conflict with the proposed withdrawal step and require the model to be reconsidered.

Advanced LearningSource changes across pregnancy6 minutes

Source changes across pregnancy

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced corpus luteum and the endometrium. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

A pathway valid soon after ovulation should not be extended unchanged through an entire pregnancy. Early hCG helps preserve corpus-luteum function, while placental hormone production later becomes a major source of support. The transition is gradual, not a switch at one exact classroom date. When interpreting a hypothetical loss of one source, first identify the developmental interval and whether another source is contributing. The same perturbation can have different consequences at different times.

Before predicting a source-removal effect, locate the case within development. The contribution of another source changes what loss of corpus-luteum function would mean. A model that is useful just after ovulation must therefore be revised as tissue contributions change.

In the related worked example: Progesterone support declines, and the maintained endometrium breaks down. The oocyte itself is not the source of the shed uterine tissue. The transition is gradual, not a universal switch on one date.

Learn · Part 4

Graphs and cycle variation

cycle variation
Differences in the timing or length of reproductive cycles; an illustrative 28-day model is not universal.
menopause
The end of recurring menstrual cycles associated with loss of ovarian follicular function; the preceding transition can involve changing cycles and hormones.

A graph communicates a comparison only when its axes and units are clear. Put cycle day on the horizontal axis. Label the vertical axis for each hormone, including whether values are concentrations or relative indices. Separate scales are suitable when signals have different units or ranges. Equal-looking heights on two relative scales do not establish equal numbers of hormone molecules.

Use the supplied six-day dataset to build four labelled series. The highest sampled estrogen value is on day 12, followed by the highest sampled LH value on day 14. Progesterone is higher on day 21 and lower on day 28. This order fits follicular development, an ovulatory signalling interval and later luteal support followed by withdrawal. The data do not identify an exact event between sparsely sampled days.

Plan the investigation before reading it. State a question about event order and predict the relationship you expect. Plot or organize every supplied value using consistent scales. Support an explanation with two named values, then compare it with the alternative claim that a peak alone gives an exact ovulation time. More frequent sampling could improve temporal resolution. It would still not make this synthetic cycle a method for predicting an individual's fertile days.

Menopause marks the end of recurring menstrual cycles through the natural loss of ovarian follicular function. The transition can involve changing cycle patterns and altered ovarian hormone support. Reduced feedback can be associated with higher pituitary FSH, so not every hormone simply falls together. This change differs from temporary variation in one cycle. A classroom graph should describe the pattern without using one symptom or a single measurement to diagnose its cause.

Worked example

Plot the supplied progesterone indices at days 2, 7, 12, 14, 21 and 28: 1, 1, 1, 2, 10 and 1. Identify the highest sampled value and a limit on timing.

  1. Put day on the horizontal axis and progesterone relative index on the vertical axis.
  2. Plot all six points with a legend if other hormones are added.
  3. Identify day 21 as the highest sampled value, while leaving the intervals between samples uncertain.

The highest sampled progesterone index is 10 on day 21. This does not establish that the true peak occurred exactly on day 21 or that its concentration exceeds another hormone measured on a different relative scale.

Stop and check

Can these relative indices be added to calculate a total hormone concentration in blood?

Compare your thinking

No. They are separate scaled indices, not compatible mass-per-volume measurements. Adding them would create an uninterpretable quantity.

Advanced LearningWhat smooth curves add6 minutes

What smooth curves add

Build from the core idea: The core explanation introduced graphs and cycle variation. Extend that idea by distinguishing the cases below.

Joining a few points with a smooth curve suggests values between observations. That is an interpolation choice, not additional measurement. Use points prominently and explain whether joining lines are guides to the eye. A useful follow-up would sample more densely around the suspected transition. This would improve temporal resolution, but it would still require information about measurement reliability and biological variation before supporting precise comparisons among individuals.

Hormone release can occur in pulses, so a single sample may miss short changes. Synthetic points also leave out differences among cycles, measurement error and some tissue responses. Repeated samples can describe variation if the method and timing are comparable. Mark the observed points separately from any inferred event; an attractive smooth curve does not remove the uncertainty between measurements.

Keep the plotted markers visible so a reader can distinguish evidence from the chosen line. Increasing sampling density near a transition can narrow its timing, but precision also depends on reliable measurements and comparable conditions. Smoothness is a drawing property, not proof of biological constancy. A curve cannot identify an unsampled peak as an observed event.

A course-authored comparison. Numerical or hypothetical cases are illustrative unless explicitly identified as supplied observations.
